comparator.name: Communication Science
comparator.academicYear: 2026–2027 prospective programme overview (year-specific pages are indicative and may change)
comparator.sourceNotes: Official prospective pages display a complete 60 EC in each of three years. Year 1 has 60 EC compulsory; year 2 has 55 EC compulsory and 5 EC free choice; year 3 has 50 EC compulsory, including a 15 EC internship and a 15 EC thesis, plus 10 EC free choice. The two free-choice components remain uninstantiated. Zero-credit academic-language work is excluded. The current year-specific pages all say 2026–2027, so this is a documented illustrative three-year pathway rather than a guaranteed cohort schedule.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Media use, information, persuasion and entertainment as communication functions
Individual, social and cultural processes behind media effects
Quantitative, qualitative and experimental communication research and bachelor thesis
Digital media platforms and communication technology
adjacent: Social media as a sustained study direction
questions: How can media communication influence health and well-being?
How do digital technologies change human interactions and information use?

alternatives.label: Closest match to communication science
alternatives.concept: A communication-science response centred on media forms, persuasion, audience psychology and empirical investigation. It combines rhetorical and media study with qualitative, statistical and experimental methods, but cannot replicate Radboud’s sustained specialist sequence, required internship or bachelor thesis.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum gives sustained attention to mediated content, effects and methods; communication science is its broad organising field.
progression: Introductory media, rhetoric, data and research precede advanced persuasion, psychology, media and audience analysis. All formal prerequisites precede dependent courses and all planned offerings match the fixed terms.

alternatives.label: Digital media and human-machine communication
alternatives.concept: A technology-focused route through social media, persuasion, visual information, human behaviour and AI-mediated interaction. Programming, mathematical methods and machine-learning courses implement the evidenced digital direction; they do not replace a specialist communication-science degree.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum contains media and rhetorical study alongside a substantial AI, data and programming sequence, which the combined label describes.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the broad communication route, this programme replaces business, organisational and qualitative-research applications with programming, mathematics, cognitive study, visual data analysis and advanced AI. The difference follows the target’s explicit social-media and human-machine directions.
progression: Introductory media, statistics and rhetoric precede advanced communication study; mathematical methods and programming precede neural-network and AI decision/optimisation courses; brain and behaviour precedes psycholinguistics. All hard prerequisites and term offerings pass.

candidates.label: Health and well-being through media influence
candidates.reason: The target explicitly mentions health effects, but this isolated application does not justify a third 24-course communication curriculum with a distinct specialist sequence at UCR; adding many biomedical courses would shift away from media research.

selection.assessment: The broad closest response covers media functions, audience effects and empirical methods. The digital route is a distinct, evidenced concentration on social media and human-machine communication and differs by more than four substantive courses. Health and well-being is an evidenced application, but the available target evidence does not support another coherent 24-course communication curriculum without substituting biomedical content for media study.

blocks: Both study forms of media experience and audience interpretation, though UCR is an introductory film and media course.
Both examine changes in media technologies and practices; Radboud frames the communication-science landscape more broadly.
Both address digital and social media technologies, although Radboud treats these within a more specialised technical curriculum.
A related UCR course appears once elsewhere in the comparison; this separately credited Radboud component has no additional one-to-one UCR course counterpart.
Both examine media representations and social consequences; UCR focuses specifically on race.
Both analyse how mediated content represents subjects and constructs meaning; UCR focuses on documentary.
Both introduce explanations of persuasive public communication; Radboud covers the wider communication-science discipline.
Both examine how persuasive messages influence audiences.
Both study psychological processes of social influence; Radboud applies them specifically to communication.
Both describe and visualise data, though UCR uses general datasets.
Both introduce research designs and methods; UCR applies them beyond communication science.
Both use qualitative inquiry into social experience; Radboud additionally requires a substantial communication research project.
Both teach inference from empirical observations and experiments; UCR uses psychology cases.
Both examine ethical implications of digital systems, with UCR focused on AI.
Both address the decisions and interactions of AI agents; UCR studies AI decisions more generally, not the full communication-science framing.
Both address reflective academic and civic formation, though the courses differ in timing and scope.
No included UCR course is dedicated to academic writing at the scope of this component.
The ten-credit content-analysis project has no directly corresponding included UCR project course.
The specialist year-one professionalisation course has no separate UCR counterpart beyond the distinct shared PPD row.
The included UCR courses do not directly address the specialist media-information component.
A methods course does not substitute for Radboud’s ten-credit empirical experiment project.
No included UCR course reproduces this distinct year-two professionalisation component.
Radboud’s five-credit free choice is genuine elective space rather than a fixed UCR course.
The selected UCR methods courses do not reproduce Radboud’s dedicated advanced statistics course.
This later professionalisation component is not the same credited course as UCR’s first-year PPD.
Radboud’s ten-credit free-choice space remains unassigned, as its actual selection is open.
Radboud requires a credited internship; the UCR schedules do not include one.
Radboud requires an independent bachelor thesis; UCR optional research is separately marked comparison-only.

notes.text: Radboud offers a sustained specialist communication-science sequence with credited empirical projects, a required internship and bachelor thesis. UCR combines media, rhetoric, psychology, research methods and digital systems but does not reproduce that entire specialist sequence.
